'''Janna J. Levin''' (born 1967) is an American [[cosmology|theoretical cosmologist]] and a professor of physics and astronomy at [[Barnard College]]. She earned a Bachelor of Arts in [[astronomy]] and [[physics]] with a concentration in philosophy at Barnard College in 1988 and a PhD in [[theoretical physics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|last=Bastek|first=Stephanie|date=April 19, 2016|title=Black Hole Blues|url=https://theamericanscholar.org/black-hole-blues/|access-date=October 14, 2021|website=[[The American Scholar (magazine)|The American Scholar]]|publisher=[[Phi Beta Kappa Society]]}}</ref> Much of her work deals with looking for evidence to support the proposal that our universe might be finite in size due to its having a nontrivial [[topology]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Levin |first=Janna |title=In space, do all roads lead to home? |url=http://plus.maths.org/issue10/features/topology/ |date=January 1, 2000|magazine=[[Plus Magazine]] |accessdate=9 August 2012}}</ref>  Other work includes [[black holes]] and [[chaos theory]]. She joined the faculty at Barnard College in January 2004 and is currently the Claire Tow Professor of Physics and Astronomy.

==Biography==
Levin was born to [[Yiddish]]-speaking Jewish parents in Texas.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Levin, Janna|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/levin-janna|access-date=2021-10-14|website=[[Encyclopedia.com]]}}</ref> Her grandparents were immigrants from eastern Europe, who eventually gave up keeping [[Kashrut]].<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Levin|first1=Janna|last2=Tippett|first2=Krista|date=January 10, 2008|title=Mathematics, Purpose, and Truth|url=https://onbeing.org/programs/janna-levin-mathematics-purpose-and-truth/|access-date=2021-10-14|website=[[On Being]]|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Kaufman|first=Eli|date=May 17, 2016|title=Janna Levin and Black Hole Blues|url=http://blogs.timesofisrael.com/janna-levin-and-black-hole-blues/|access-date=2021-10-14|website=Times of Israel - Blogs|language=en-US}}</ref> She describes her household as mostly not religious (Levin was not brought to synagogue and was not [[Bar and bat mitzvah|bat mitzvah]]ed). Levin attended [[Columbia University]] for her bachelor's degree and [[MIT]] for her Ph.D., graduating in 1993. In 2002 she held a research fellowship at Cambridge University (England).<ref>"Cosmic girl's chaos theory" by Anjana Ahuja, ''The Times'' (London) part 2, February 11, 2002, page 10</ref>

Janna Levin is a professor of physics and astronomy at Barnard College of Columbia University with a grant from the Tow Foundation. She researches [[black holes]], the cosmology of extra dimensions, and [[gravitational wave]]s in the shape of [[spacetime]].  In addition she is the director of sciences at [[Pioneer Works]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Levin|first1=Jenna|title=Bio|url=http://jannalevin.com/bio-and-contact/|accessdate=14 January 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Janna Levin|url=https://www.barnard.edu/profiles/janna-levin|publisher=Barnard College|accessdate=14 January 2018}}</ref>

Levin is the author of the popular science book ''How the Universe Got Its Spots: Diary of a Finite Time in a Finite Space''. In 2006, she published ''[[A Madman Dreams of Turing Machines]]'', a novel of ideas recounting the lives and deaths of [[Kurt Gödel]] and [[Alan Turing]].<ref name="myerson2007">{{cite journal |last=Myerson |first=Sylvie |title=Janna Levin in conversation with Sylvie Myerson |journal=[[Brooklyn Rail]] |date=September 2007 |url=http://brooklynrail.org/2007/09/express/janna-levin-with-sylvie-myerson}}</ref>

Levin has written a series of essays to accompany exhibitions at several galleries in England, including the [[Ruskin School of Drawing and Fine Art]] and the [[Hayward Gallery]].<ref name=art>{{cite web|url=http://www.jannalevin.com/art.html |title=The Office of Janna Levin: Art |publisher=Janna Levin |accessdate=2012-08-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120308174733/http://www.jannalevin.com/art.html |archive-date=2012-03-08 }}</ref>  Levin was featured on ''[[Talk of the Nation]]'' on July 12, 2002.<ref name=interviews>{{cite web|url=http://www.jannalevin.com/interviews.html |title=The Office of Janna Levin: Video + Audio |publisher=Janna Levin |accessdate=2012-08-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903061838/http://www.jannalevin.com/interviews.html |archive-date=2012-09-03 }}</ref> She appeared as a guest on [[Stephen Colbert]]'s [[Comedy Central]] show ''[[The Colbert Report]]'' on August 24, 2006.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.colbertnation.com/the-colbert-report-videos/73484/august-24-2006/janna-levin |title=Janna Levin – The Colbert Report |work=[[Comedy Central]] |publisher=[[Viacom (2005–present)|Viacom]] |date=2006-08-24 |accessdate=2012-08-10}}</ref>  She also appeared as the featured guest on the ''[[Speaking of Faith]]'' radio show on February 22, 2009, where she discussed her book ''A Madman Dreams of Turing Machines'' with the show's host [[Krista Tippett]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://speakingoffaith.publicradio.org/programs/mathandtruth/index.shtml |title=Mathematics, Purpose, and Truth &#124; On Being |work=[[Speaking of Faith]] |date=2012-05-31 |accessdate=2012-08-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705022302/http://speakingoffaith.publicradio.org/programs/mathandtruth/index.shtml |archive-date=2010-07-05 }}</ref>
Levin presented "The sound the universe makes" on [[TED.com]] on March 1, 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/janna_levin_the_sound_the_universe_makes |title=The sound the universe makes: Janna Levin on TED.com |publisher=TED Blog |date=2011-03-15 |access-date=2012-08-10}}</ref>  She was named a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] in 2012.<ref name=bio>{{cite web|url=http://www.jannalevin.com/bio.html |title=The Office of Janna Levin: Bio + Photos |publisher=Janna Levin |accessdate=2012-09-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120529060256/http://www.jannalevin.com/bio.html |archive-date=2012-05-29 }}</ref>
[[File:Janna Levin no Fronteiras do Pensamento São Paulo 2019 (48688788956) (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Levin in 2019]]
Her book ''Black Hole Blues and Other Songs from Outer Space'' was published in March, 2016. The book is about the history of the [[Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory]] and the 2015 discovery of [[gravitational waves]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Bastek|first=Stephanie|date=April 19, 2016|title=Black Hole Blues|url=https://theamericanscholar.org/black-hole-blues/#.WW9872NstHg|website=[[The American Scholar (magazine)|The American Scholar]]|publisher=[[Phi Beta Kappa Society]]}}</ref> In a review of the book published in ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'', British astrophysicist [[John Gribbin]] wrote, "This is a splendid book that I recommend to anyone with an interest in how science works and in the power of human imagination and ability."<ref>{{cite news | last =Gribbin | first =John | title =A Billion Year-Old Postcard: The collision of two black holes produced more than a trillion times the power of a billion Suns.| newspaper = [[Wall Street Journal]]| date =March 25, 2016 | url =https://www.wsj.com/articles/a-billion-year-old-postcard-1458933723| accessdate =March 25, 2016 }}</ref> In January 2018 she hosted [[Nova (American TV program)|Nova's]] award-winning episode "Black Hole Apocalypse."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/video/black-hole-hunter-janna-levin/ |title=Black Hole Hunter: Janna Levin |website=PBS |date=January 10, 2018 }}</ref>

==Personal life==

Levin did not officially graduate from high school, as she was in a serious car accident and hospitalized for a time.<ref name=bio />

Levin is the parent of two children, a son born in 2004 and a daughter born in 2007. Her partner, Warren, is a musician.<ref>"Cosmic girl's chaos theory" by Anjana Ahuja, The Times (London) part 2, February 11, 2002, page 10</ref>
